title: Green Card Backlog Traps Nearly One Million Indians as EB-2 Wait Hits 179 Years
excerpt: NFAP analysis shows Indians account for 79% of the US employment-based immigration backlog, with new EB-2 applicants facing a potential 179-year wait under current law.
body:
• Nearly one million Indians are waiting in the EB-1, EB-2, and EB-3 green card categories, accounting for 79% of the total US employment-based backlog of 1.26 million
  • An Indian national filing an EB-2 petition in January 2026 or later faces a potential 179-year wait; EB-3 applicants face 38 years
  • The backlog grew 21% since 2020 despite 280,000 extra green cards being issued during that period
  • The per-country cap of 7% means India receives the same visa allocation as countries like Iceland and Luxembourg

Close to one million Indian nationals are now stuck in the US employment-based green card backlog, making up roughly four out of every five people waiting across the country's top three employment categories, according to a new analysis by the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

The numbers are stark. NFAP estimates that as of December 2025, nearly one million Indians were waiting in the EB-1, EB-2, and EB-3 preference categories — out of a total estimated backlog of 1,264,495. The EB-2 category, which covers workers with advanced degrees or exceptional ability, accounts for the bulk: an estimated 731,566 Indians. Another 213,414 were in the EB-3 queue.

A Wait Measured in Lifetimes

The backlog has reached a point where wait times defy any practical planning. An Indian national whose employment-based petition or labor certification was filed in January 2026 or later could face a potential wait of 179 years for permanent residence in the EB-2 category and 38 years in EB-3, according to NFAP's calculations.

"For individuals in the EB-2 or EB-3 category from India, the wait is more likely to be measured in decades than in years."

— National Foundation for American Policy report

The August 2026 Visa Bulletin underscores the gridlock. To file an adjustment-of-status application, Indian applicants need a priority date earlier than October 15, 2022, for EB-1 and January 1, 2014, for EB-3. The EB-2 category is listed as entirely unavailable this month, after showing a cutoff date of September 1, 2013, in the June 2026 bulletin.

Why Indians Bear the Brunt

Two structural constraints in US immigration law drive the disproportionate impact on Indian nationals. The annual employment-based visa cap stands at 140,000 — a number set by Congress in 1990 that includes both the principal worker and eligible dependents. Dependents typically consume half or more of available slots.

The per-country ceiling compounds the problem. Under Section 202(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, no single country can receive more than 7% of total employment-based visas. India, with its large population of highly skilled professionals, effectively receives the same allocation as nations like Iceland and Luxembourg.

The math makes the accumulation inevitable. In fiscal 2016, US Citizenship and Immigration Services approved 47,601 EB-2 applications from Indian nationals — an estimated 98,594 people including dependents. But only 4,407 Indians received permanent residence in that category that year. In a single fiscal year, more than 90,000 people were added to the backlog.

More Green Cards Still Not Enough

The backlog grew even as the US issued significantly more employment-based green cards than usual. Between fiscal years 2020 and 2024, a total of 980,460 employment-based green cards were issued — roughly 280,000 more than the expected 700,000, according to NFAP. Unused family-sponsored visa numbers during the pandemic rolled over to employment-based categories, creating the surplus. It was not enough to dent the accumulated queue.

The overall backlog increased from 1,048,342 in April 2020 to 1,264,495 by December 2025 — a rise of 216,153 people, or 20.6%. NFAP warns the number could exceed two million by 2040 without changes to US immigration law.

What It Means for Indian Professionals in America

For hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals already working in the US, the backlog carries real daily consequences. Many remain on H-1B temporary status for years, their ability to stay and work contingent on extensions and continued compliance. The labor certification process alone adds years of delay: the Department of Labor reports average PERM processing times of 403 days for analyst review and 290 days for audit review as of August 2026.

"These long waiting times for green cards create significant hardships for individuals and their families and undermine the ability of companies to attract and retain talent in America."

— Stuart Anderson, Executive Director, NFAP

Legislative proposals to address the backlog have not gained traction. A 2022 measure that would have exempted PhD holders in science and technology fields and master's degree holders in critical industries from numerical limits was considered during the CHIPS and Science Act negotiations but was dropped from the final legislation. Without reform, NFAP says, the fundamental math remains: demand far exceeds the number of employment-based immigrant visas available each year, and the per-country limits ensure Indians bear the heaviest burden.
nri_angle: Directly impacts nearly one million Indian professionals and families waiting for US permanent residence, with new applicants facing multi-generational waits.
